## Reproducibility and analytical choice {#one-number-the-whole-class}

<!-- The last fragment differs by format: the decks that teach the
     specification menu (deck: {menu: true} in their YAML) name it, the others
     list the choices. -->

:::: {.none}
::: {.fragment}
Everyone who chose the same analyst got the same value, to the third decimal, and every recorded value came back. That is reproducibility, and it is the easy R.
:::

::: {.fragment}
You all ran the *same code*. The five Multi100 analysts each wrote their own, on the same public file, and came back with five different numbers and two different verdicts.
:::

::: {.fragment}
None of them was careless. They made different choices[, and the options that they chose from make up the **menu**]{.content-visible when-meta="deck.menu"}[ about **which names** to compare, **which emails** to count and **which test** to run]{.content-visible unless-meta="deck.menu"}.
:::
::::

::: notes
Look at what just happened. Different people, on different machines, chose different analysts, and everyone who chose the same analyst landed on the same number, agreeing with the record to the third decimal. That is reproducibility, and notice how cheap it was: you ran code that the course wrote, on a file that anyone can download, so of course you got the recorded numbers back. Reproducibility is the easy R. [pause] Now set that against the five analysts themselves. They had the same public file, each wrote their own analysis, and they came back with five different numbers, and not even the same verdict on whether the data supported the claim. Not one of them was careless: four of the five published their scripts on the OSF, and they are competent pieces of work. So the spread is not a matter of quality. It is a matter of the choices that each of them made.
:::
